stem: A production service's output quality drops on a day with no deploy and no prompt change. The model is specified by an alias. What is the remediation?

options.text: Add post-processing to restore the previous output shape
Pin an explicit dated model identifier and gate future upgrades on an eval re-run
Lower the temperature to stabilize the output
Move the alias into an environment variable

explanation: An unpinned alias lets the underlying model change without a deploy, matching quality shifting on a day nothing shipped. Moving the alias to an environment variable relocates the config without stopping the drift.
author: legacy

stem: Which file should be committed so a team shares the same Claude Code permission rules and hooks?

options.text: .claude/settings.local.json
.claude/settings.json
A .env file in the repository root
The user-level ~/.claude/settings.json

explanation: Project settings.json is the shared, committed configuration. The .local.json variant is personal and gitignored, user-level settings apply to one developer, and secrets never belong in a committed file.
author: legacy

stem: How should prompts be managed in a production Claude application?

options.text: Embedded as string literals near the code that uses them, for locality
Versioned in source control with review, tied to eval results, and rollback-capable
Stored in a database and edited directly in production for fast iteration
Regenerated by the model at deploy time to stay current

explanation: Prompts are code. Version them, review them, tie each version to eval results, and make rollback as fast as a code rollback. Editing directly in production removes the review and eval gate.
author: legacy

stem: A platform team distributes an internal plugin through a private marketplace. To signal a new release, they bump the version field in the marketplace catalog entry from 1.2.0 to 1.3.0, but forget that the plugin's own plugin.json manifest still declares version 1.2.0. Team members run the plugin update command afterward.

options.text: Users receive version 1.3.0, because the marketplace entry takes precedence for signaling new releases
Claude Code throws a version-conflict error and blocks the update until the two files agree
Users keep the cached 1.2.0 build, because Claude Code resolves the version from plugin.json first, silently masking the marketplace entry's value
Claude Code merges the two version strings and installs whichever one is numerically higher

explanation: Claude Code resolves a plugin's version from its own plugin.json manifest before consulting the marketplace catalog entry, and does so without warning, so a stale manifest version silently masks a version bump made only in the marketplace entry. Assuming the marketplace entry wins gets the precedence backwards. There is no conflict error raised when the two disagree; the mismatch is silent, which is exactly the danger the mechanism creates. There is no merge-and-take-higher behavior either — one field wins outright, and it isn't the marketplace entry.
author: v1-new

stem: A model an application depends on moves from Active to Deprecated status. Anthropic names a recommended replacement and sets a retirement date roughly 90 days out. The on-call engineer's instinct is to switch the pinned model identifier in every environment, including production, the same day the deprecation notice arrives.

options.text: Leave the deprecated model pinned everywhere until the retirement date, to avoid any risk of a behavior change before then
Switch every environment, including production, immediately, since deprecated models are already less reliable
Remove the explicit model pin entirely and switch to an alias, so future deprecations are absorbed automatically
Test the replacement model against the existing eval suite first, then roll the pin forward once results clear the bar, well before the retirement date

explanation: Configuration-management discipline gates any pinned-model change on an eval re-run before promoting it to production, and does so with enough runway before a hard deadline to absorb a failed evaluation. Waiting until the retirement date risks a forced, untested cutover with no time to react if the replacement regresses. Switching immediately without running the eval suite reintroduces exactly the 'quality shifted with no controlled deploy' risk that pinning exists to prevent. Removing the pin in favor of an alias trades one drift problem for a worse one, since an alias updates on Anthropic's schedule rather than on a schedule the team controls.
author: v1-new

stem: A team lead wants two things guaranteed on every Claude Code invocation across the team, with no reliance on the model choosing to comply: a specific destructive shell command must always be blocked outright, and a formatter script must always run after every file edit. Select the two configuration mechanisms that actually guarantee this behavior regardless of what Claude decides.

options.text: A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude never to run that command and to run the formatter after every edit
A permissions.deny rule in the shared, committed project settings.json blocking the command
A PostToolUse hook configured in settings.json that runs the formatter after every file edit
A longer, more detailed instruction appended to every request asking Claude to follow both rules

explanation: Permission rules and hooks configured in settings.json are enforced by the Claude Code client itself, independent of what the model decides to do on any given turn, which is exactly what 'guaranteed, no exceptions' requires. A CLAUDE.md instruction is delivered as context the model reads and tries to follow, not a control the client enforces, so however clearly it's worded it remains a request rather than a guarantee. Appending a longer instruction to every request has the identical failure mode as the CLAUDE.md option: rewording or relocating a plain-language instruction doesn't change the fact that it's advisory, not deterministic.
author: v1-new
